articles.title: Goody Goody review – intriguing natural childbirth horror lurches into demonic occult blowout
articles.summary: After Samantha Robinson decides a forest cabin in deep winter is the perfect spot to bear her child, it’s going to be a very bad shift for the doula and midwife. Conception, pregnancy and childbirth are defining human experiences, and so remain perennial themes for horror, from Rosemary’s Baby to…
body: Goody (Samantha Robinson) is in the pool, ready for battle, soaking in good vibes beamed at her by husband Jayson (Colby Hollman), his doula sister Candace (Zoe Renee) and their rock, midwife Sarah (Colleen Foy). But shaken by weirdly spaced contractions, Sarah takes Jason aside and admits that she has a bad feeling. It’s not purely premonition: a flashback reveals, in contrast to the new-age love-in around the tub, Goody’s insistence against Sarah’s advice that she give birth in winter at their forest cabin. The midwife fears it will make going to hospital too difficult should anything go wrong – and only agrees to supervise because Goody will probably go ahead solo if she pulls out.

Creamer starts out by layering telling details that insinuate the stifling boho perfectionism ruling this household: a faux Freewheelin’ Bob Dylan cover featuring the couple, their disdain for teabags, the cloying veneer of positivity. He films the damning flashback with psychological finesse to show Jayson’s status as junior partner; back on the natal frontline, Candace sometimes slips into a grandstanding bolshiness that threatens to tip Sarah’s carefully nurtured equilibrium out of balance.

articles.title: Israeli minister threatens to strip Israeli film-makers of citizenship over Gaza documentary NAZA
articles.summary: Miki Zohar accuses Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of ‘treason against the state’ ‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence.
body: Israel’s culture minister has called for the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of NAZA, a documentary about the country’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, to be stripped of their citizenship, accusing them of “treason against the state”.
NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza.

In the film, the Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor spoke to 24 different Israeli military or intelligence whistleblowers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza that have killed tens of thousands of civilians. In one interview, a source claims that approval had been given to kill 500 NAZA in order to kill one Hamas member.
The 80-minute documentary won a special jury prize at this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receiving a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record.

articles.title: Lee Chang-dong’s Films Head to Netflix Worldwide After ‘Possible Love’ Wins Silver Lion at Venice
articles.summary: Netflix will expand its lineup of Lee Chang-dong films worldwide, following the Silver Lion (Grand Jury Prize) win for “Possible Love” at the Venice Film Festival. The expansion will let viewers everywhere explore titles including “Secret Sunshine” and “Peppermint Candy.” “Possible Love,” Lee’s…
body: Rollout timing differs by market, and some territories will get the films with subtitle options covering as many as six languages, Korean among them.

Lee debuted as a director with “Green Fish” in 1997, going on to build a filmography that also includes “Peppermint Candy,” “Oasis,” “Secret Sunshine,” “Poetry” and “Burning.” His work has drawn top honors on the festival circuit: “Oasis” earned him a directing prize at Venice in 2002, and “Poetry” took the screenplay award at Cannes in 2010. Lee’s newest distinction came at the Toronto Film Festival ‘s 51st edition, where he became the first Korean filmmaker to receive its Ebert Director Award.

“Possible Love” centers on two couples: one formed by a man who has lost his job and his wife, the other by a woman who directs documentaries and her husband. Their lives intersect during the making of a documentary, drawing out desires and struggles each had kept hidden. The film stars Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong, and is South Korea’s submission for the best international feature film category at the 99th Academy Awards.

articles.title: Love of Your Life review – Margaret Qualley eats, grieves and loves in Amazon’s transporting saga
articles.summary: Toronto film festival: the actor gives one of her best performances to date in a smoothly made globe-trotting drama of a woman’s life after the loss of her husband. There’s a jump scare about 30 minutes into the glossy romantic drama Love of Your Life that’s about as effective as anything you’ll…
body: The film is focused on the life and loves of Maya (Margaret Qualley), a twentysomething Boston nurse who meet-cutes with the nerdy and idiosyncratic Felix (Gabriel Basso) during the purchase of a nightstand. We follow the initial giddy rush of their courting as they progress all the way to an impromptu wedding over the course of a few years, marked by Maya’s change in age announced in text. But just as we’re about to process the unsettling introduction of Felix using Chekhov’s inhaler, a news report interrupts the sunny tone. Spoiler: it’s March 2020.

It’s Eat, Grieve, Love which is by no means a bad thing given how few mainstream films attempt to zero in on the vast lives of women both in and out of relationships (I remain a staunch defender of Ryan Murphy’s prettified yet emotionally resonant adaptation of a book I am otherwise unbothered by). There’s also a bit of How to Be Single (minus the bawdy humour), another film I’m often defending or at least drawing attention to and there’s something admirably ambitious about settling in with a female protagonist for such a long period of time to see how they live and learn after a loss many of us couldn’t imagine surviving.

articles.summary: “The Odyssey” continued its voyage at the summit of the South Korean box office during the weekend of Sept. 11–13. body: Superhero tentpole “ Spider-Man: Brand New Day ” was tin third place in its seventh outing, generating $544,123 from 84,719 admissions over the frame. The film accounted for 7% of the frame, bringing its local gross to $68.7 million from 8,930,413 admissions.

“The Drama” opened in fourth place, earning $223,340 from 29,512 admissions over the three-day window across 616 screens. Since its Sept. 9 premiere, the release has collected $404,575 from 53,631 total admissions.

Local family road-trip drama “The Journey to Gyeongju” took fifth place, generating $124,071 from 17,206 admissions. Directed by Kim Mi-jo and starring Lee Jung-eun, Gong Hyo-jin, Park So-dam, Lee Yeon, and Byun Yo-han, the revenge-tinged family narrative pushed its haul to $2.3 million from 332,960 viewers.
“Power Ballad” placed sixth, taking $110,283 from 15,277 admissions and has gathered $633,484 from 89,399 admissions since its Sept. 2 debut.

articles.title: China Box Office: ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’ Stays on Top as ‘The Odyssey’ Crosses $100 Million
articles.summary: Dirty Monkeys’ war comedy-drama “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” held the number one spot at the mainland China box office for the fifth straight frame, collecting RMB52.9 million ($7.8 million) over the Sept. 11–13 weekend, according to data from Artisan Gateway.
body: Pearl Studio’s animated fantasy comedy “ All Wishes Come True! ” was in third position in its ninth frame, generating $4 million. Directed by Mu Zhengyang, the enduring family hit has reached a cumulative total of $283.4 million since its July 18 debut.

In fourth place Universal’s “ The Odyssey ” crossed the century mark in China, adding $3.5 million for a cumulative total of $102.9 million. Crossing the $100 million threshold pushes the film well past the China runs of “Oppenheimer,” “Tenet,” and “Inception,” leaving it second in Christopher Nolan’s local catalog only to the $122 million lifetime gross of “Interstellar.”

Rounding out the top five, Phoenix Legend Films’ time-bending fantasy romance “My Tomorrow, Your Yesterday” opened with $1.7 million over its two-day debut frame. Directed by Xiang Guoqiang and adapted from Takafumi Nanatsuki’s Japanese novel, the film stars Bi Wenjun as an architectural restorer who falls in love with a medical student played by He Landou, only to uncover that her timeline flows in reverse to his, leaving them with an expiring window together.

articles.title: Lenore review – incel’s obsession with online influencer turns into anatomy of dislocated digital-age mindset
articles.summary: Digital-age Australian psychodrama tracks the shut-in mania of dangerously disaffected male fan, but doesn’t get inside his mind. If the parasocial phenomenon is a kind of hell, then Max Wren, protagonist of this Australian digital-age psychodrama, resides in the ninth circle.
body: Sam’s intrusion, and that of the pair of police who later come knocking, are relayed as bewilderingly loud violations of Max’s sanctuary. This kind of simple sonic effect might have hit hard on stage (the film is adapted from an unproduced play) – but Ward doesn’t progress into a style that bottles the 21st-century digital cacophony. Instead his film is awkwardly divided between sterile theatrical exchanges and Max’s soliloquies at his stack of tech, and didactic rants from the metaverse in which Lenore discourses about no man owning her.

Only Max’s mental disintegration, zoning out as Leonore appears to communicate directly with him, threatens a fertile piercing of this barrier à la David Cronenberg; and it comes to fruition in a final beatification that turns out to be anything but saintly. Ward can clearly diagnose our dislocated mindset – but without him finding an idiom to match, it seems unlikely that the average TikTok-addled scrollhead will have the patience to hear the final judgment.

articles.title: Netflix to Stream Lee Chang-dong’s Films Globally as ‘Possible Love’ Awards Campaign Heats Up
articles.summary: All six of the Korean auteur’s previous features, including ‘Burning,’ ‘Peppermint Candy’ and ‘Secret Sunshine,’ are rolling out across various territories ahead of the global streaming launch of ‘Possible Love’ on Nov. 6.
body: Netflix is offering global cinephiles a deeper dive into the work of Korean master Lee Chang-dong as it ramps up the awards-season rollout of his acclaimed new drama Possible Love.

Fresh off Possible Love ’s Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize win at the Venice Film Festival over the weekend, the streamer said Monday that it is expanding the availability of all six of Lee’s previous features across various international markets. The rollout includes Green Fish (1997), Peppermint Candy (1999), Oasis (2002), Secret Sunshine (2007), Poetry (2010) and Burning (2018), although availability and timing vary by country. articles.title: A Bland ‘60 Minutes’ Season Premiere Suggests a Limited Bari Weiss Effect (So Far)
articles.summary: Led by familiar faces Lesley Stahl, Jon Wertheim and Norah O'Donnell, Sunday night's episode was often mediocre, but not in any shocking or dramatically different ways.
body: There have been months of controversy, outrage and general conversation regarding alterations to CBS’ 60 Minutes franchise under new CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss. But the venerable newsmagazine returned Sunday night to start its 59th season with a premiere that will probably offer very, very limited confirmation to both the pessimistic and optimistic biases espoused by pundits on the left and right.

The reality is that the 99.999 percent of 60 Minutes viewers who watched the show because they were too lazy to change the channel after CBS’ late NFL game ended, who watched out of tradition or casual curiosity or complacency, will not have noticed anything even vaguely notable or different in Sunday night’s premiere. Someone could write a thousand words pretending that aspects of Sunday’s 60 Minutes were earthshaking or infuriating or disgraceful, when the truth is that the premiere was mediocre but rarely in shocking or horrifying or new ways.
